tagline: Rolling hills and river towns along highways near the Buffalo Trace
intro: Indiana's Historic Pathways crosses rural countryside, rolling hills and forests, linking the lower Ohio Valley with the Mississippi Valley. The Federal Highway Administration lists it as a 250-mile National Scenic Byway, recommends a day for the trip and emphasizes its historic districts and Indiana history. Between Shoals and Loogootee, US 50 and US 150 share a road beside the East Fork White River.

The FHWA traces the corridor’s story from bison to pioneer and stagecoach travel, then to modern highways. US 150 roughly parallels the Buffalo Trace between New Albany and Vincennes. The highway numbers came later: in 1926, parts of US 50 and US 150 replaced State Road 5. US 150 initially ran from Shoals to New Albany; its 1934 extension carried the number farther northwest along US 50.

For a westbound journey on the US 150 branch, start at New Albany and continue through Palmyra to Paoli’s courthouse square. Continue to Shoals, where US 150 meets US 50, then follow their shared route through Loogootee and past Washington toward Vincennes. The road broadens from two lanes east of I-69 to a divided four-lane highway farther west. Vincennes brings the journey to the Wabash River.

moments.title: Paoli
moments.text: At Paoli, the highway meets a courthouse square: US 150 passes Courthouse Square, which surrounds the Orange County Courthouse. The town was laid out in 1816. Wikipedia’s town history describes early Paoli as a Quaker community that helped transport enslaved people from the South to Canada through the Underground Railroad. It also identifies the Pioneer Mothers Memorial Forest as a surviving fragment of southern Indiana’s virgin oak forest, a distinction associated with Paoli in the twentieth century.

moments.title: Shoals
moments.text: Jug Rock stands outside Shoals, separated from a nearby cliff by erosion along fractures in the sandstone. In his 1871 geological report, E. T. Cox described a 42-foot rock capped by a projecting flat layer called the “stopper.” The formation is now part of an Indiana Department of Natural Resources nature preserve, and the Shoals High School teams take their Jug Rox name from it. Through town runs the East Fork White River; its mussels supplied the material for Shoals’ early-twentieth-century mother-of-pearl buttons. House Rock stands opposite Jug Rock, a companion feature in the East Fork valley.

moments.title: Vincennes
moments.text: The territorial capitol at Vincennes is a simple two-story frame building, moved to its present site in 1949. French fur traders founded Vincennes on the lower Wabash in 1732, decades before it became a territorial capital. Vincennes became the Indiana Territory’s capital in 1800 and remained so until the government moved to Corydon in 1813. Built between 1800 and 1805, the capitol now forms part of a row of buildings across from Vincennes University. The capitol is part of a state historical site and lies within the Vincennes Historic District.
